name: Diffusion of Innovations
one_line_summary: Rogers' S-curve model of how innovations spread through innovators, adopters, and laggards.
extended_summary: Diffusion of Innovations is a substantial empirical research tradition codified by Everett Rogers in his 1962 Diffusion of Innovations (revised through five editions, the fifth posthumously in 2003). Rogers synthesized research from rural sociology (the diffusion of hybrid corn, foundational Iowa State work by Bryce Ryan and Neal Gross in 1943), public health, education, and other fields to characterize how innovations spread through populations over time. The framework's central claim is that adoption typically follows an S-shaped cumulative curve, with adopters categorized into five groups based on time of adoption: Innovators (~2.5% — venturesome, willing to take risks); Early Adopters (~13.5% — opinion leaders, role models); Early Majority (~34% — deliberate, adopt before average); Late Majority (~34% — skeptical, adopt under social pressure); and Laggards (~16% — traditional, adopt last). Five attributes of innovations affect adoption rate: relative advantage, compatibility, complexity, trialability, observability. The framework substantially shaped marketing strategy (Geoffrey Moore's Crossing the Chasm extends Rogers's adopter categories), public health intervention design, agricultural extension, and educational technology adoption. The empirical foundation is unusually strong by social-science standards, with thousands of replications across domains and decades.
originators: Everett M. Rogers (codification); Bryce Ryan and Neal Gross (foundational hybrid-corn study, 1943); rural sociology tradition
year_or_decade: 1943 (Ryan-Gross hybrid corn study); 1962 (Rogers Diffusion of Innovations 1st ed); 2003 (5th edition, posthumous)
core_components: S-curve cumulative adoption; Five adopter categories: Innovators, Early Adopters, Early Majority, Late Majority, Laggards (with population percentages); Five innovation attributes affecting adoption rate: relative advantage, compatibility, complexity, trialability, observability; Communication channels (mass media for awareness; interpersonal for persuasion); Opinion leaders' role in early-majority adoption; Connection to network theory and social influence; Substantial empirical foundation across domains
primary_use_case: Marketing strategy and product launch (foundation for Geoffrey Moore's Crossing the Chasm extension to high-tech product adoption); public health intervention design and adoption; agricultural extension and technology transfer; educational technology adoption; foundation for many implementation-science frameworks; reference framework in sociology and communication studies.
common_criticisms: Adopter categories are somewhat artifactual — the five categories are statistical conveniences rather than discrete population types, and individuals can adopt different innovations at different points in the curve; pro-innovation bias: framework assumes adoption is good, when many innovations are appropriately rejected; equality bias: framework underweights how structural inequalities affect access to innovations; laggard label has been argued to be pejorative when 'laggards' may have legitimate reasons for non-adoption; recall bias in retrospective adoption studies; cross-cultural variation in adoption patterns is substantial; framework works better for technological innovations than for behavior changes or organizational practices; commercial use sometimes overclaims predictive power that Rogers himself was careful about.
primary_sources: Ryan, B. & Gross, N.C. (1943). 'The Diffusion of Hybrid Seed Corn in Two Iowa Communities', Rural Sociology; Rogers, E.M. (1962, 5th ed. 2003). Diffusion of Innovations; Moore, G.A. (1991). Crossing the Chasm (high-tech extension)
siblings: Strength of Weak Ties; Social Capital Theory

name: Structural Functionalism
one_line_summary: Society as an integrated system of parts each serving stability-maintaining functions.
extended_summary: Structural Functionalism is the macrosociological tradition treating society as an integrated system of interconnected parts (institutions, norms, roles, structures), each contributing to the stability and reproduction of the whole through specific functions. The tradition descends from Émile Durkheim's foundational 19th-century work on social facts and the division of labor (The Division of Labor in Society, 1893; Suicide, 1897), substantially developed by British social anthropologists Bronisław Malinowski and A.R. Radcliffe-Brown, and elaborated as the dominant mid-20th-century American sociological framework by Talcott Parsons (The Social System, 1951; AGIL framework — Adaptation, Goal attainment, Integration, Latency) and Robert K. Merton (manifest vs latent functions; functional alternatives; dysfunctions, in Social Theory and Social Structure, 1949). The framework's analytical commitments include explaining social patterns by their functional contributions to social stability, treating institutions as adapted to system needs, and studying society as analogous to a biological organism with interdependent parts. Structural functionalism dominated American sociology through the 1950s but was substantially displaced from the 1960s onward by Conflict Theory, Symbolic Interactionism, and other competing frameworks that critiqued its conservative implications, its inability to explain conflict and change, and its tendency toward teleological reasoning.
originators: Émile Durkheim (foundational); Bronisław Malinowski, A.R. Radcliffe-Brown (British anthropological development); Talcott Parsons (American codification); Robert K. Merton (refinement and extension)
year_or_decade: 1893-1897 (Durkheim foundational); 1920s-30s (British anthropology); 1950s (Parsons, Merton dominance); subsequent decline
core_components: Society as integrated system; Functions of social parts (institutions, roles, norms); Manifest functions (intended) vs latent functions (unintended; Merton); Functional alternatives; Dysfunctions (Merton); AGIL framework (Parsons): Adaptation, Goal attainment, Integration, Latency; Organic analogy; Equilibrium tendency; Mid-20th-century American sociological dominance and subsequent displacement
primary_use_case: Foundational macrosociological tradition; substantial historical influence on sociology, anthropology, and political science; framework for analyzing institutional functions and social stability; reference framework in sociological theory education; basis for some contemporary neo-functionalist work (Alexander, Luhmann's systems theory descended in part from this tradition).
common_criticisms: Conservative implications: explaining institutions by their functions tends to legitimate the status quo, treating existing arrangements as functional necessities rather than contingent power arrangements; cannot adequately explain social conflict, change, or revolution — phenomena that conflict theorists argued were central to social life rather than aberrations; teleological reasoning: 'X exists because it serves function Y' assumes system-level needs that drive selection of social forms, a problematic assumption; functional alternatives are often unspecified; failure to account for dysfunctions and contradictions; cultural variation makes universal functional claims problematic; substantial displacement from 1960s onward by competing frameworks; American mid-20th-century framing reflects Cold War-era anxieties about social stability that subsequent generations have questioned.
primary_sources: Durkheim, E. (1893). The Division of Labor in Society; Parsons, T. (1951). The Social System; Merton, R.K. (1949, multiple editions). Social Theory and Social Structure

name: Conflict Theory
one_line_summary: Society as an arena of struggle between groups over scarce resources and power, rooted in Marx.
extended_summary: Conflict Theory is the macrosociological tradition treating society as fundamentally constituted by conflict between groups with opposing interests over scarce material resources, power, status, and ideological dominance — directly opposed to Structural Functionalism's emphasis on integration and stability. The tradition's foundational figure is Karl Marx (with Friedrich Engels), whose analysis of class conflict between bourgeoisie and proletariat in capitalism (Communist Manifesto 1848; Capital Volume I 1867) provided the foundational frame, with Max Weber's pluralist extension (multiple bases of conflict — class, status, party — in Economy and Society, 1922) substantially complementing Marx. American conflict theory emerged in the 1950s and 1960s through Lewis Coser (functions of social conflict, 1956), C. Wright Mills (the power elite, 1956), and Ralf Dahrendorf, with substantial subsequent development by Pierre Bourdieu (cultural capital, symbolic violence), feminist theorists (gender as conflict axis), critical race theorists, and others. The framework's analytical commitments include explaining social patterns by underlying conflicts and power asymmetries, treating institutions as instruments of dominance, and studying social change through conflict resolution. Conflict theory substantially displaced functionalism in American sociology from the 1960s onward and remains one of the principal macrosociological traditions.
originators: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels (foundational); Max Weber (pluralist extension); Lewis Coser, C. Wright Mills, Ralf Dahrendorf (mid-20th-century American development); Pierre Bourdieu, feminist and critical-race theorists (subsequent extension)
year_or_decade: Marx mid-19th century; Weber early 20th century; American conflict theory 1950s-60s; ongoing extensions
core_components: Society as arena of conflict between groups; Conflict over resources, power, status, ideology; Marxist class analysis (bourgeoisie vs proletariat); Weberian pluralist extension (class, status, party); Connection to ideology and false consciousness; Bourdieu's capital extensions (economic, cultural, social, symbolic); Feminist and critical-race extensions; Distinction from functionalism on the question of social order and change; Foundation for critical theory tradition
primary_use_case: Macrosociological analysis particularly of inequality, power, and social change; foundation for substantial work in stratification, race, gender, and political sociology; reference framework in critical theory and political-economy traditions; basis for many activist-oriented sociological practices; foundation for class analysis in policy and labor studies.
common_criticisms: Reductive variants overemphasize material conflict and underweight non-conflictual sources of social order (cooperation, shared meaning, affection); Marxist variants face empirical challenges from welfare-state capitalism and class structures that don't follow predicted dynamics; can be deployed as ideological framework rather than empirical analysis when 'conflict' is presupposed rather than demonstrated; multiple competing axes of conflict (class, race, gender, etc.) create coordination problems for the framework; distinction between productive social conflict (Coser) and pathological conflict can collapse in radical variants; like functionalism, can become a totalizing frame that explains everything by its preferred mechanism; tension between explanatory and political projects of conflict-theoretic work.
primary_sources: Marx, K. & Engels, F. (1848). The Communist Manifesto; Marx, K. (1867). Capital, Volume I; Weber, M. (1922, posthumous). Economy and Society; Coser, L.A. (1956). The Functions of Social Conflict; Mills, C.W. (1956). The Power Elite
siblings: Structural Functionalism; Symbolic Interactionism; Critical Theory

name: Symbolic Interactionism
one_line_summary: Mead and Blumer's view of society as constituted through meaning-laden interaction.
extended_summary: Symbolic Interactionism is the microsociological tradition treating society as constituted through symbolic communication and meaning-making in everyday interaction, with the self emerging through social interaction rather than preceding it. The tradition's foundational figure is George Herbert Mead, whose Mind, Self, and Society (1934, posthumous, compiled from student notes) articulated the genesis of self through 'taking the role of the other' (the I-Me distinction; the generalized other; the gestural conversation that becomes language), drawing on William James, John Dewey, and Charles Horton Cooley. Herbert Blumer (Mead's student at Chicago) coined the term 'symbolic interactionism' in 1937 and codified the framework's three premises in 1969: humans act toward things based on the meanings they have for them; meanings arise through social interaction; and meanings are modified through interpretive processes. Erving Goffman's dramaturgical extension (separately enriched in this batch) gave symbolic interactionism its most influential contemporary form. The framework dominated 20th-century microsociology through the Chicago School and provided substantial methodological foundation for ethnography, grounded theory, and qualitative research. Distinct from but related to social constructionism (which often draws on symbolic interactionist insights at scale).
originators: George Herbert Mead (foundational, posthumous Mind Self Society); Herbert Blumer (term coinage, codification); Charles Horton Cooley, William James, John Dewey (precursors); Chicago School tradition
year_or_decade: Mead's lectures 1900s-1930s; 1934 (Mind, Self, and Society); 1937 (Blumer coins term); 1969 (Blumer Symbolic Interactionism)
core_components: Three premises (Blumer): humans act toward things based on meanings; meanings arise through social interaction; meanings modified through interpretation; Mead's I-Me distinction; Generalized other; Taking the role of the other; Significant symbols; Ethnographic and qualitative methods; Connection to Chicago School; Foundation for grounded theory (Glaser, Strauss); Distinction from macro-structural approaches
primary_use_case: Foundational microsociological tradition; methodological foundation for ethnography and grounded theory; analysis of identity formation, role-taking, and everyday social life; foundation for Goffman's dramaturgy and other interactionist extensions; influence on social psychology, particularly the symbolic interactionist tradition within social psychology distinct from cognitive social psychology; reference framework in sociology and communication studies.
common_criticisms: Microsociological focus underweights structural and material conditions that shape interactional possibilities; meaning-making framing can be politically conservative when it ignores how power shapes which meanings prevail; methodological commitment to qualitative fieldwork limits comparison with quantitative traditions; coherence across the tradition's various branches (Chicago School, Iowa School, dramaturgical, ethnomethodological-adjacent) is contested; risk of voluntarism (treating interaction as fully creative when it operates within substantial constraints); empirical generalization from particular ethnographic studies is challenging; tradition's twentieth-century American framing limits cross-cultural application; tension with cognitive science accounts of meaning that operate at sub-symbolic levels.
primary_sources: Mead, G.H. (1934, posthumous). Mind, Self, and Society; Blumer, H. (1969). Symbolic Interactionism: Perspective and Method; Cooley, C.H. (1902). Human Nature and the Social Order
siblings: Goffman's Dramaturgy; Looking-Glass Self; Social Construction of Reality

name: Goffman's Dramaturgy
one_line_summary: Social life analyzed as theatrical performance with frontstage and backstage regions.
extended_summary: Erving Goffman's dramaturgical sociology was articulated in The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life (1959), with subsequent elaborations across Asylums (1961), Behavior in Public Places (1963), Interaction Ritual (1967), and Frame Analysis (1974). Goffman analyzes social interaction through the extended metaphor of theatrical performance, with key concepts including: front stage (where the performance is given to an audience) and back stage (where the performer prepares and relaxes); team performances (groups of performers cooperating to sustain a definition of the situation); impression management (the active work of presenting oneself in particular ways); face-work (managing one's social standing in interactions); and the moral character of social order (interactants implicitly cooperate to sustain shared definitions, with substantial social damage when they don't). Goffman's contribution to symbolic interactionism is microsociological in focus but distinctive in the sustained dramatic metaphor and the emphasis on social order as ritually accomplished moment-by-moment. Frame Analysis (1974) extended the framework to analyze how participants identify what kind of activity is happening (the frame) and how frames can be transformed or breached. Goffman's influence has extended substantially beyond sociology — into communication theory, organizational studies, and contemporary discussions of online self-presentation in social media research.
originators: Erving Goffman
year_or_decade: 1959 (The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life); ongoing development through 1974 (Frame Analysis)
core_components: Front stage and back stage regions; Performance and team performance; Impression management; Face-work and face-saving; Definition of the situation; Frames and frame analysis (1974 extension); Civil inattention; Stigma management (Stigma, 1963); Total institutions (Asylums, 1961); Distinction from cynical and sincere performance; Moral character of social order; Application to online self-presentation in contemporary research
primary_use_case: Microsociological analysis of everyday interaction; foundation for substantial work on identity management, organizational impression management, communication theory; reference framework in sociology, communication, and contemporary social-media research; basis for analyses of stigma management and self-presentation; influence on professional communication training and customer-service-design frameworks.
common_criticisms: Theatrical metaphor can suggest cynicism about social interaction (everyone is performing) when Goffman's analysis is more nuanced about the moral character of performance; underweights structural conditions shaping which performances are possible and credible (gender, race, class affect who can credibly perform what); microsociological focus does not connect well to macro-level questions of power and inequality; conceptual proliferation across Goffman's books creates which-concept-when ambiguity; some applications stretch the dramaturgical metaphor beyond its analytical force; cross-cultural applicability of specific concepts (face-work, civil inattention) varies; contemporary online-self-presentation extensions sometimes overstate continuities with Goffman's original face-to-face frame; the tradition's American mid-20th-century framing shows in particular concept choices.
primary_sources: Goffman, E. (1959). The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life; Goffman, E. (1963). Stigma: Notes on the Management of Spoiled Identity; Goffman, E. (1974). Frame Analysis: An Essay on the Organization of Experience

name: Foucault's Power-Knowledge
one_line_summary: Power and knowledge as inseparable, jointly producing subjects through discourse and discipline.
extended_summary: Michel Foucault's framework of power-knowledge (pouvoir-savoir) was developed across his major works of the 1970s — Discipline and Punish (1975), The History of Sexuality Volume 1 (1976), and the lecture courses at the Collège de France (1970-1984, posthumously published) — as a fundamental rethinking of how power operates in modern societies. Against the 'juridical' model of power as something held by sovereigns and exercised through prohibition, Foucault articulated power as productive, capillary (operating through countless local sites rather than centralized institutions), and inseparable from knowledge: regimes of truth establish what can be known and said, and these regimes are themselves effects of power that simultaneously enable new forms of power. Key concepts include: disciplinary power (operating through surveillance, normalization, examination — the panopticon as paradigmatic image); biopower (power operating on populations rather than individual bodies, through statistics, public health, demography); governmentality (the conduct of conduct, art of governing through shaping subjects' self-conduct); and discourse (regulated systems of statements that produce objects of knowledge and corresponding subjects). Foucault's frameworks have had enormous influence on sociology, history, political theory, gender studies, postcolonial studies, and critical scholarship across humanities and social sciences. His later work on ethics and care of the self (volumes 2-3 of History of Sexuality, the late lecture courses on parrhesia and the hermeneutics of the subject) complicates simpler readings of Foucault as exclusively a theorist of domination.
originators: Michel Foucault
year_or_decade: 1975 (Discipline and Punish); 1976 (History of Sexuality Vol 1); 1970-1984 lecture courses (College de France, posthumously published)
core_components: Power-knowledge inseparability (pouvoir-savoir); Productive rather than only repressive power; Capillary power (countless local sites); Disciplinary power (surveillance, normalization, examination, panopticon); Biopower (populations, statistics, demographics); Governmentality (conduct of conduct); Discourse and regimes of truth; Subject-formation through power-knowledge; Genealogy and archaeology as method; Late ethics (care of self, parrhesia)
primary_use_case: Critical theory and post-structuralist sociology; foundation for substantial work in gender studies, postcolonial studies, queer theory, science and technology studies, governmentality studies; analysis of modern institutions (prisons, hospitals, schools, militaries); influence on political theory, critical legal studies, and contemporary social criticism; reference framework in much critical scholarship across humanities and social sciences.
common_criticisms: Conception of power as everywhere risks emptying the concept of analytical content — if everything is power, the concept distinguishes nothing; tension between Foucault's apparent normative critique of disciplinary power and his refusal to ground critique in normative principles; difficulty translating power-knowledge analysis into political agency or strategy; specific historical claims (about the prison, about sexuality) have been challenged by historians; Habermas's substantial critique that Foucault's position is performatively self-undermining (truth-claims about regimes of truth); poststructuralist suspicion of the subject creates difficulties for political and ethical thought that Foucault's later work addressed unevenly; commercial and academic appropriation has produced 'Foucault as toolkit' use that loses the systematic philosophical commitments; cross-cultural application of European-history-grounded analysis is contested.
primary_sources: Foucault, M. (1975). Surveiller et punir / Discipline and Punish: The Birth of the Prison; Foucault, M. (1976). Histoire de la sexualité, Vol I / The History of Sexuality, Vol I; Foucault's lecture courses at the Collège de France (1970-1984, published posthumously)

name: Weber's Bureaucracy
one_line_summary: Ideal-type bureaucracy characterized by hierarchy, rules, impersonality, and technical expertise.
extended_summary: Max Weber's analysis of bureaucracy was developed in Economy and Society (1922, posthumous, multiple translations) within his broader theory of rationalization — the historical process by which traditional and charismatic authority are progressively displaced by rational-legal authority grounded in formal rules and procedures. Weber's ideal-type bureaucracy comprises six characteristics: hierarchical structure with clear lines of authority; specialized division of labor with defined competencies; written rules and procedures governing action; selection and advancement based on technical qualifications; impersonal application of rules without favoritism; separation of office from officeholder (the office is institutional, not personal property). Bureaucracy in this sense represents the most technically efficient form of organization for large-scale coordination, surpassing traditional and charismatic alternatives. Weber's analysis was deeply ambivalent: rationalization was the engine of modern productivity and impartiality, but he also feared its 'iron cage' effects on human meaning and freedom — the disenchantment of the world, the displacement of values by means-ends calculation, the bureaucratic personality reduced to functional execution. The framework has been substantially extended (Robert Michels's iron law of oligarchy; Selznick's institutionalist extensions; James March and Herbert Simon's bounded rationality; the New Public Management critique) and remains foundational to organization theory, public administration, and political sociology.
originators: Max Weber
year_or_decade: Early 20th century (Weber's writings); 1922 (Economy and Society, posthumous)
core_components: Six ideal-type characteristics: hierarchy, specialized division of labor, written rules, technical qualification, impersonality, office-officeholder separation; Three types of authority: traditional, charismatic, rational-legal; Rationalization process; 'Iron cage' of rationality; Disenchantment of the world; Bureaucracy as technically efficient organization; Connection to Weber's broader theory of capitalism (Protestant Ethic and Spirit of Capitalism, 1905); Distinction between formal and substantive rationality
primary_use_case: Foundation of organization theory and public administration; analysis of large organizations (corporate, governmental, military, religious); reference framework in political sociology and the study of state administration; basis for substantial subsequent organizational research (Selznick, March-Simon, Crozier, DiMaggio-Powell new institutionalism); pedagogical framework in sociology, political science, and management education; influence on critique of administrative state.
common_criticisms: Ideal-type framing has been argued to underweight the actual messiness of bureaucratic practice — informal networks, workarounds, and political dynamics often matter more than formal structures (informal organization tradition: Roethlisberger-Dickson, Crozier); rules-oriented framing produces 'goal displacement' (Merton) where following rules becomes substitute for achieving purposes; cross-cultural variation in bureaucratic forms has been substantial — Weber's analysis reflects German bureaucratic experience; New Public Management and post-bureaucratic alternatives argue Weber's framework is dated for contemporary fluid, networked organizations; the 'iron cage' critique can be deployed as romantic anti-bureaucracy without engaging the genuine alternatives bureaucracy was historically displacing; tension between Weber's analytical neutrality and his evident ambivalence about rationalization; the framework's dominance has produced bureaucracy-as-default-explanation in some applied contexts.
primary_sources: Weber, M. (1922, posthumous, multiple translations). Economy and Society; Weber, M. (1905). The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism

name: Structuration Theory
one_line_summary: Giddens' account of structure and agency as recursively constituted.
extended_summary: Structuration Theory was developed by Anthony Giddens across multiple works in the 1970s and 1980s, with the canonical statement in The Constitution of Society: Outline of the Theory of Structuration (1984). The theory addresses the long-standing structure-agency problem in social theory — whether social phenomena are best explained by structural conditions (functionalism, structuralism, Marxism) or by individual action (interpretive sociology, methodological individualism) — by arguing that structure and agency are mutually constitutive: structure is both the medium and outcome of action. Giddens's 'duality of structure' holds that structures (rules and resources) exist only insofar as they are reproduced through situated action, and action is possible only because actors draw on existing structures. Key concepts include: agency as the capacity to do otherwise; rules and resources as the elements of structure; routine action and the practical consciousness that produces social order; reflexive monitoring of action; time-space distanciation (modern social systems extending across time and space); and the dialectic of control (even subordinates have some power over their superordinates). Structuration theory has had substantial influence in sociology, organization studies (particularly through Wanda Orlikowski's adaptations to information systems and DeSanctis-Poole's adaptive structuration theory), geography, and other social sciences, though it has drawn criticism for being more programmatic than empirically operationalizable.
originators: Anthony Giddens
year_or_decade: 1976 (New Rules of Sociological Method); 1979 (Central Problems in Social Theory); 1984 (The Constitution of Society)
core_components: Duality of structure (structure as medium and outcome of action); Structure as rules and resources; Agency as capacity to do otherwise; Practical consciousness vs discursive consciousness; Routine action and ontological security; Reflexive monitoring of action; Time-space distanciation; Dialectic of control; Distinction from structural and interpretivist alternatives; Adaptation to organization studies (Orlikowski, DeSanctis-Poole)
primary_use_case: Sociological theory bridging structure-agency divide; foundation for substantial work in organizational studies on technology and structuration (Orlikowski's structurational model of technology); reference framework in geography, political science, and information systems; basis for some methodological approaches that aim to capture both structural and agentic dimensions; teaching framework in social-theory education.
common_criticisms: Programmatic rather than operational — Giddens articulates how structure and agency are mutually constituted but provides limited methodological guidance for empirical research, and structuration-informed empirical work has been argued to be sociology-as-usual with structuration vocabulary added; Margaret Archer's morphogenetic alternative (1995) argues that Giddens conflates structure and agency in ways that lose analytical power, and that they should be analytically separated to study their interaction; the theory has been argued to be programmatic synthesis rather than substantive new theory; concepts proliferate without clear empirical operationalization; the dialectic of control claim about subordinates always having some power has been argued to underweight genuine domination; commercial appropriations in organization studies have varied in fidelity to Giddens's framework; tension between Giddens's social-theoretic ambitions and his later popular-public-intellectual work on Third Way politics.
primary_sources: Giddens, A. (1979). Central Problems in Social Theory; Giddens, A. (1984). The Constitution of Society: Outline of the Theory of Structuration; Archer, M.S. (1995). Realist Social Theory: The Morphogenetic Approach (alternative)

name: Actor-Network Theory
one_line_summary: Latour and Callon's framework treating humans and non-humans as symmetric actants in networks.
extended_summary: Actor-Network Theory was developed in the late 1970s and 1980s within science and technology studies (STS) by Bruno Latour, Michel Callon, and John Law, with foundational formulations in Latour's Science in Action (1987), Callon's 'Some Elements of a Sociology of Translation' (1986, the scallops-and-fishermen paper), and Law's various works. The framework's distinctive commitment is generalized symmetry — treating humans and non-humans (technologies, materials, microorganisms, documents, instruments) as ontologically symmetric 'actants' that participate in heterogeneous networks. Social phenomena are produced by networks of human and non-human actants whose interactions constitute particular outcomes; what we call 'society' or 'science' or 'technology' is the trace of these networks, not a substrate behind them. Key concepts include: translation (the process by which actors enroll others into networks); obligatory passage points (positions that all network participants must traverse); inscriptions (documents, traces, representations that mobilize and stabilize networks); black-boxing (treating complex networks as unitary actors). Latour's later work, particularly Reassembling the Social (2005), articulated ANT as a method of describing rather than explaining the social. ANT has been substantially influential in STS, organization studies, geography, anthropology, and information systems, though it has drawn substantial critique for what some see as ontological flattening of the human-nonhuman distinction and for its political ambiguity.
originators: Bruno Latour; Michel Callon; John Law (foundational); subsequent contributors including Madeleine Akrich, Annemarie Mol, Wiebe Bijker (related but distinct SCOT framework)
year_or_decade: Late 1970s-80s development; 1986 (Callon scallops paper); 1987 (Latour Science in Action); 2005 (Latour Reassembling the Social)
core_components: Generalized symmetry (humans and non-humans as actants); Networks of heterogeneous actants; Translation (enrolling actors into networks); Obligatory passage points; Inscriptions (documents, traces, representations); Black-boxing (complex network as unitary actor); Methodological commitment to following actors and tracing networks; Distinction from structural sociology (no underlying social substrate); STS origins; Latour's later anthropology of moderns work
primary_use_case: Science and technology studies; analysis of technological controversies, scientific practice, and innovation; organization studies of technology integration; geographic and urban studies; anthropology of materiality; information systems research; reference framework in many post-positivist social science traditions; basis for some practical methodological approaches in qualitative research.
common_criticisms: Ontological symmetry between humans and non-humans is contested — critics including Marxist and humanist sociologists argue that flattening human and non-human agency loses crucial analytical distinctions; political ambiguity: ANT's descriptive commitment to following actors makes it difficult to articulate critique or normative position (though Latour's later work substantially addressed this); methodological prescription to 'follow the actors' provides limited guidance and can produce ANT-flavored ethnography that uses the vocabulary without the analytical commitments; the framework's prose style (particularly Latour's) is famously demanding; risk of voluntarism (everything is constructed in networks) without adequate accounts of why some networks stabilize and others don't; Bijker's SCOT (Social Construction of Technology) provides alternative without ANT's generalized-symmetry commitments; commercial and academic appropriations vary widely in fidelity.
primary_sources: Callon, M. (1986). 'Some Elements of a Sociology of Translation: Domestication of the Scallops and the Fishermen of St Brieuc Bay'; Latour, B. (1987). Science in Action; Latour, B. (2005). Reassembling the Social: An Introduction to Actor-Network-Theory
siblings: Foucault's Power-Knowledge; Social Construction of Reality

name: Critical Theory
one_line_summary: Marxist-derived tradition critiquing culture, ideology, and instrumental rationality.
extended_summary: Critical Theory in its specific Frankfurt School sense designates the tradition of social theory developed at the Institut für Sozialforschung (Institute for Social Research) in Frankfurt from 1923 onward, with its distinctive program articulated by Max Horkheimer in 'Traditional and Critical Theory' (1937). The first generation — Horkheimer, Theodor Adorno, Herbert Marcuse, Walter Benjamin, Erich Fromm — developed Marxist-derived analyses substantially extended by engagement with Freud, Hegel, and Weber, exiled to Columbia University from 1934-1953, and produced foundational works including Adorno-Horkheimer's Dialectic of Enlightenment (1944), Adorno's Minima Moralia (1951), Marcuse's One-Dimensional Man (1964), and the Authoritarian Personality study (1950). The framework's central commitments include: critique of instrumental rationality and the culture industry as mechanisms of domination in advanced capitalism; analysis of fascism and authoritarian personality; integration of Marx and Freud; pessimism about the working class as historical agent of emancipation; and an open-ended dialectical method oriented to immanent critique rather than positive program. The second generation, principally Jürgen Habermas (separately enriched in Theory of Communicative Action), substantially reformulated the project around communicative rationality. Third-generation figures including Axel Honneth (recognition theory) continue the tradition. 'Critical theory' more broadly is sometimes used to encompass critical race theory, feminist theory, postcolonial theory, and other normatively-engaged social theory traditions, but the Frankfurt-School sense remains distinct.
originators: Max Horkheimer (program articulation, 'Traditional and Critical Theory' 1937); Theodor Adorno; Herbert Marcuse; Walter Benjamin; Erich Fromm; Jürgen Habermas (second generation); Axel Honneth (third generation)
year_or_decade: 1923 (Frankfurt Institute founded); 1937 (Horkheimer foundational essay); 1944 (Dialectic of Enlightenment); subsequent generations through 21st century
core_components: Critique of instrumental rationality; Culture industry critique (Adorno-Horkheimer); Authoritarian personality (Adorno et al. 1950); Negative dialectics; Immanent critique; Integration of Marx and Freud; Aesthetic theory (Adorno); Habermas's communicative-rationality reformulation; Honneth's recognition theory; Distinction from traditional theory (purportedly value-free); Distinction from positivism
primary_use_case: Social and cultural theory; critique of mass culture and consumer capitalism; foundation for substantial subsequent critical traditions; analysis of fascism and authoritarian movements; reference framework in cultural studies, media studies, and political theory; basis for ongoing tradition of normatively-engaged social criticism; influence on aesthetics and music theory (Adorno).
common_criticisms: First-generation pessimism about emancipatory possibilities (particularly Adorno-Horkheimer's Dialectic of Enlightenment) has been argued to lead to political quietism — if administered society is total, what is to be done?; cultural-critique framing has been critiqued as elitist (the Adornian aesthetic preferences for difficult modernist art over popular forms); Habermas's substantial reformulation suggests the first-generation framework was inadequate, but the relation between generations is contested; critical theorists' Frankfurt-school institutional context shaped specific commitments that don't always travel well; tension between immanent critique and positive program; challenges in distinguishing 'critical theory' (Frankfurt-school sense) from broader 'critical' theory traditions; popular conflation with critical race theory and other distinct traditions creates confusion; American and European receptions diverge substantially.
primary_sources: Horkheimer, M. (1937). 'Traditional and Critical Theory'; Adorno, T.W. & Horkheimer, M. (1944). Dialectic of Enlightenment; Marcuse, H. (1964). One-Dimensional Man; Adorno, T.W. et al. (1950). The Authoritarian Personality
siblings: Conflict Theory; Foucault's Power-Knowledge; Theory of Communicative Action

name: Social Construction of Reality
one_line_summary: Berger and Luckmann's account of how shared meanings come to feel objectively given.
extended_summary: The Social Construction of Reality was articulated by Peter Berger and Thomas Luckmann in their 1966 book of the same name, synthesizing Alfred Schutz's phenomenological sociology, George Herbert Mead's symbolic interactionism, and Karl Mannheim's sociology of knowledge. Berger and Luckmann's central thesis is that what people experience as objective reality is socially constructed through three dialectically related moments: externalization (humans produce a social world through their activity); objectivation (the produced world acquires apparent objectivity, confronting individuals as fact); and internalization (the objectivated world is taken back into individual consciousness through socialization). The framework analyzes how institutions arise from habitualized action, how legitimation systems explain and justify the institutional order, how reality is maintained through everyday conversation and 'plausibility structures,' and how individuals are socialized into reality through primary and secondary socialization. The book's enormous influence — it remains one of the most-cited sociology texts of the 20th century — extends across sociology, anthropology, education, and beyond, providing the foundational vocabulary for the broader 'social constructionist' or 'social constructivist' approaches that became prominent across humanities and social sciences from the 1980s onward, including in science studies (where social construction of scientific facts became contested), gender studies (gender as socially constructed), and critical race theory.
originators: Peter L. Berger; Thomas Luckmann; intellectual antecedents in Alfred Schutz, George Herbert Mead, Karl Mannheim
year_or_decade: 1966 (foundational book)
core_components: Three dialectical moments: externalization, objectivation, internalization; Habitualization and institutionalization; Legitimation and symbolic universes; Plausibility structures; Primary and secondary socialization; Reality-maintenance through conversation; Connection to Schutz's phenomenological sociology; Distinction between everyday reality and other 'finite provinces of meaning'; Foundation for broader social-constructionist tradition
primary_use_case: Foundational text in sociology of knowledge and the broader social-constructionist tradition; analysis of institutions, identity formation, and shared reality; reference framework across sociology, anthropology, education, organization studies; foundation for substantial subsequent work in science studies, gender studies, critical race theory, and other constructionist traditions; basis for many qualitative-research methodologies.
common_criticisms: Strong-constructionist readings have been argued to undermine the analytical force of distinguishing between socially constructed phenomena (gender categories, professional identities) and physical phenomena (gravity, virus transmission) — the science-wars debates of the 1990s tested how far social construction extends; Ian Hacking's The Social Construction of What? (1999) provided substantial taxonomy of different constructionist claims; the tradition has been argued to be politically ambivalent — descriptive social construction can support either status quo (reality is as it is, socially constructed) or progressive change (reality could be otherwise); methodological challenge of identifying when something is 'really' socially constructed vs only described as such; Berger himself substantially modified his views in later work; the popular 'everything is socially constructed' usage substantially exceeds Berger-Luckmann's actual claims; cross-cultural application of European-Christian-modernity-grounded analysis is contested.
primary_sources: Berger, P.L. & Luckmann, T. (1966). The Social Construction of Reality: A Treatise in the Sociology of Knowledge; Hacking, I. (1999). The Social Construction of What?
siblings: Symbolic Interactionism; Goffman's Dramaturgy; Actor-Network Theory

name: Strength of Weak Ties
one_line_summary: Granovetter's finding that loose acquaintances bridge networks more effectively than close ties.
extended_summary: The Strength of Weak Ties was articulated by Mark Granovetter in his 1973 American Journal of Sociology paper of that name, with the empirical foundation in his Harvard dissertation research on how professional and managerial workers in Newton, Massachusetts found their jobs. Granovetter found, contrary to common assumption, that most successful job-finders had heard of their job through 'weak ties' (acquaintances) rather than 'strong ties' (close friends and family) — and developed the theoretical explanation that close ties tend to share the same network and information, while weak ties bridge across otherwise-disconnected social networks, providing access to non-redundant information. The argument's structural form is general: weak ties are more likely to be 'bridges' between densely-connected clusters, and information flowing through bridges reaches farther than information staying within clusters. Granovetter's 1985 'Economic Action and Social Structure: The Problem of Embeddedness' substantially extended this work into economic sociology. The strength-of-weak-ties result has been one of the most empirically replicated findings in sociology, with substantial extensions to network theory (Ronald Burt's structural holes, 1992), social capital research (Putnam's bridging vs bonding), and contemporary network science. The result has had substantial practical influence on job-search advice, organizational network analysis, and social-media platform design (LinkedIn explicitly markets weak-tie value).
originators: Mark S. Granovetter
year_or_decade: 1973 (foundational AJS paper); 1974 (Getting a Job book); 1985 (embeddedness extension)
core_components: Strong ties (close friends, family) vs weak ties (acquaintances); Strong ties tend to share networks (redundant information); Weak ties more likely to bridge networks (non-redundant information); Job-search empirical foundation; Bridges as structurally important network positions; Connection to Burt's structural holes; Connection to Putnam's bridging social capital; Network-theoretic generalization beyond original domain; Substantial empirical replication across contexts
primary_use_case: Network analysis and social network theory; job-search advice and labor-market analysis; organizational network analysis (information flow, innovation diffusion); social capital research; foundation for substantial subsequent network-science work; influence on LinkedIn and other professional social-network platform design; basis for many practical recommendations about networking and information seeking.
common_criticisms: Original empirical context (white-collar professionals in 1970s Boston) may not generalize to all labor markets — recent research suggests strong ties matter more for some demographics and industries than the original framing suggests; the dichotomy between strong and weak ties oversimplifies a continuum, with substantial subsequent work refining; gendered and racialized differences in network access mean that weak-tie advantages depend on having access to weak ties in productive networks; social-media-era weak ties may differ qualitatively from the 1970s acquaintance ties Granovetter studied; some recent research (e.g., Aral and colleagues' large-scale LinkedIn experiment, 2022) suggests strength-of-weak-ties claims need updating for digital networks; framework's elegance and citability have produced applications that exceed the empirical evidence; the bridging-vs-bonding distinction can be politically loaded when weak ties are presumed always more valuable.
primary_sources: Granovetter, M.S. (1973). 'The Strength of Weak Ties', American Journal of Sociology; Granovetter, M.S. (1974). Getting a Job: A Study of Contacts and Careers; Granovetter, M.S. (1985). 'Economic Action and Social Structure: The Problem of Embeddedness', American Journal of Sociology
siblings: Social Capital Theory; Diffusion of Innovations

name: Social Capital Theory
one_line_summary: Putnam's framework of bonding, bridging, and linking ties as productive resources.
extended_summary: Social Capital Theory analyzes the productive value of social relationships and networks — the 'capital' that exists in social ties and the trust, norms of reciprocity, and information they enable. The contemporary concept has multiple lineages: Pierre Bourdieu's articulation of social capital as one of four forms of capital (economic, cultural, social, symbolic) in his 1986 'The Forms of Capital'; James Coleman's 1988 'Social Capital in the Creation of Human Capital' (American Journal of Sociology) treating social capital as a public good produced through ongoing relations; and most influentially Robert Putnam's Bowling Alone (2000) and earlier Making Democracy Work (1993, on Italian regional governments), which substantially popularized the concept and developed the bonding (within-group) vs bridging (across-group) vs linking (across-power-asymmetry) distinctions. Putnam's American story documented declining civic engagement, organizational membership, and informal social ties from the mid-20th century, arguing that this decline in social capital had substantial consequences for democratic functioning. The framework has had enormous influence in sociology, political science, public health (social capital as health determinant), economic development, and international development. Empirical operationalization remains contested — measures vary substantially across studies — and Bourdieu's, Coleman's, and Putnam's framings have substantively different theoretical commitments that the shared vocabulary obscures.
originators: Pierre Bourdieu (continental theoretical foundation); James S. Coleman (American sociology development); Robert D. Putnam (substantial popularization); precursors including Lyda Judson Hanifan (1916), Jane Jacobs (1961)
year_or_decade: Hanifan 1916 (precursor); 1986 (Bourdieu); 1988 (Coleman); 1993 (Putnam Italy book); 2000 (Putnam Bowling Alone)
core_components: Social ties as productive resource; Trust and norms of reciprocity; Information and influence flows through networks; Bonding (within-group) vs bridging (across-group) vs linking (across-power-asymmetry); Putnam's American civic-engagement decline thesis; Bourdieu's capital framework (economic, cultural, social, symbolic); Coleman's public-good treatment; Multiple competing operationalizations and measures; Connection to civic engagement, democracy, and public health
primary_use_case: Sociological and political science research on civic engagement, democracy, and community; public health (social capital as health determinant in 'social determinants of health' framework); economic development and international development; reference framework for community-development practice; foundation for many measurements of community wellbeing; basis for substantial policy discussion about social cohesion.
common_criticisms: Multiple substantively different framings (Bourdieu's, Coleman's, Putnam's) share vocabulary but differ in theoretical commitments — Bourdieu's framework treats social capital as a means of class reproduction, while Putnam's treats it as a public good, with different political implications; empirical operationalization is genuinely contested — measures vary substantially across studies, complicating cumulative empirical work; Putnam's American civic-decline thesis has been challenged on measurement and causality grounds (some declines are real, others reflect changing forms of association rather than overall decline); 'capital' metaphor risks reducing relational and ethical dimensions of social life to functional resources; bonding vs bridging distinction can be politically loaded; 'social capital' has been argued to obscure power dynamics — communities with strong bonding social capital among insiders can be exclusionary; cross-cultural application is uneven.
primary_sources: Bourdieu, P. (1986). 'The Forms of Capital'; Coleman, J.S. (1988). 'Social Capital in the Creation of Human Capital', American Journal of Sociology; Putnam, R.D. (2000). Bowling Alone: The Collapse and Revival of American Community
siblings: Strength of Weak Ties; Diffusion of Innovations

name: Looking-Glass Self
one_line_summary: Cooley's account of self formed through perception of how others see us.
extended_summary: The Looking-Glass Self was articulated by Charles Horton Cooley in his 1902 Human Nature and the Social Order, providing one of the foundational accounts of social self-formation in American sociology and a key intellectual antecedent of symbolic interactionism. Cooley's central claim is that the self is not formed through introspection or solitary reflection but through imagining how we appear to others — a three-step process: (1) we imagine how we appear to a particular person; (2) we imagine that person's judgment of that appearance; (3) we develop a feeling about ourselves (pride, mortification, etc.) based on that imagined judgment. The 'looking-glass' metaphor captures how others function as mirrors in which we see ourselves: the self is genuinely social rather than only social-influenced. Cooley's account influenced George Herbert Mead's subsequent more-elaborate theory of the social self (Mind, Self, and Society, 1934, with the I-Me distinction and generalized other), and through Mead substantially shaped symbolic interactionism. Empirical research on the looking-glass self has produced mixed results — there is good evidence that imagined-self-appraisal influences self-perception, but the correspondence between actual others' views and our imagined version of those views is often weaker than Cooley's account suggests. The framework remains foundational in sociological social psychology and has influenced contemporary discussions of social-media self-presentation.
originators: Charles Horton Cooley
year_or_decade: 1902 (Human Nature and the Social Order)
core_components: Three-step process: imagine how we appear to other; imagine other's judgment; develop self-feeling (pride, mortification, etc.); Self as fundamentally social; Looking-glass metaphor; Connection to Mead's later social-self theory (I-Me, generalized other); Foundation for symbolic interactionism; Distinction between actual others' views and our imagined version of them; Application to identity, self-esteem, and contemporary social-media research
primary_use_case: Foundational sociological account of self-formation; reference framework in symbolic interactionist tradition and sociological social psychology; analysis of identity, self-concept, and reflected appraisals; influence on contemporary social-media self-presentation research; teaching tool in introductory sociology and social psychology; foundation for understanding dynamics of stigma, recognition, and identity.
common_criticisms: Empirical research shows that the correspondence between actual others' views and our imagined version of those views (the 'looking glass') is often weaker than Cooley's account suggests — we imagine others' judgments based partly on our self-views, producing a circularity that reduces the framework's explanatory force; cross-cultural variation in self-construal (Markus-Kitayama on independent vs interdependent self-construal) suggests the looking-glass model reflects Western individualist assumptions about how self relates to others; the framework underweights non-reflective and unconscious sources of self; subsequent more-elaborate theories (Mead, contemporary identity theory) have largely subsumed the looking-glass self into broader frameworks; popular usage often invokes the term loosely without engaging Cooley's specific three-step structure.
primary_sources: Cooley, C.H. (1902). Human Nature and the Social Order; Cooley, C.H. (1909). Social Organization

name: Strain Theory
one_line_summary: Merton's framework of deviance arising from gap between cultural goals and legitimate means.
extended_summary: Robert K. Merton's Strain Theory was articulated in his 1938 American Sociological Review paper 'Social Structure and Anomie' and elaborated in Social Theory and Social Structure (1949). Merton extended Émile Durkheim's concept of anomie (normative breakdown) to analyze deviance in American society as arising from a structural disjunction between culturally-prescribed goals (success, wealth, status) and the institutional means available to achieve them — when culture intensely emphasizes goals while structures restrict legitimate access to means, individuals experience strain that produces five characteristic adaptations: Conformity (accept goals, accept means — modal); Innovation (accept goals, reject legitimate means — much crime, fraud); Ritualism (reject goals, retain means — bureaucratic compliance without ambition); Retreatism (reject both — addiction, vagabondage); Rebellion (substitute new goals and means). Strain theory was substantially influential in mid-20th-century criminology and sociology of deviance, providing a structural account of criminality alternative to individual-pathology framings. Robert Agnew's General Strain Theory (1992) substantially extended Merton's framework by adding additional sources of strain (loss of valued stimuli, presentation of negative stimuli) beyond goal-blockage, and by attending to emotional mediation between strain and deviance. Strain theory remains a major framework in criminology, though much subsequent work has challenged or refined its specific predictions.
originators: Robert K. Merton (foundational); Émile Durkheim (anomie precursor); Robert Agnew (General Strain Theory extension)
year_or_decade: 1938 (Merton 'Social Structure and Anomie'); 1949 (Social Theory and Social Structure); 1992 (Agnew General Strain Theory)
core_components: Structural disjunction between culturally-prescribed goals and institutional means; Five adaptations: Conformity, Innovation, Ritualism, Retreatism, Rebellion; Connection to Durkheim's anomie; Strain theory of deviance and crime; Agnew's General Strain Theory extension (additional sources of strain beyond goal-blockage; emotional mediation); Distinction from individual-pathology accounts of crime; Application to American Dream and social-mobility concerns; Influence on criminology and sociology of deviance
primary_use_case: Criminology and sociology of deviance; analysis of crime and delinquency; foundation for substantial work on crime causation; reference framework in criminology education; basis for some criminological policy discussions about opportunity and social mobility; integration with other criminological frameworks (control theory, learning theory); influence on social-policy thinking about crime prevention through opportunity expansion.
common_criticisms: Original framework better predicts property crime than violent crime; assumes uniform cultural goals across society, when sub-cultural variation in goal-emphasis is substantial; Agnew's General Strain Theory addressed many critiques but added complexity that reduces parsimony; cross-cultural variation in strain-deviance relationships is substantial; class biases in original framing — focus on lower-class crime to the exclusion of white-collar crime that may have similar structural roots; competing criminological frameworks (control theory, learning theory, labeling theory, life-course theory) capture aspects strain theory misses; quantitative tests of strain theory have produced mixed empirical results; risk of structural-determinist readings that under-emphasize agency and choice in deviance.
primary_sources: Merton, R.K. (1938). 'Social Structure and Anomie', American Sociological Review; Merton, R.K. (1949). Social Theory and Social Structure; Agnew, R. (1992). 'Foundation for a General Strain Theory of Crime and Delinquency', Criminology

name: Labeling Theory
one_line_summary: Deviance as a social product of labeling rather than an inherent property of acts.
extended_summary: Labeling Theory was substantially developed in the 1960s within the symbolic interactionist tradition, principally through Howard S. Becker's Outsiders: Studies in the Sociology of Deviance (1963), Edwin Lemert's Social Pathology (1951, primary vs secondary deviance), and the broader 'societal reaction' tradition. The framework's central reframing is that deviance is not a quality of acts in themselves but the application of social labels to acts and actors — 'deviant behavior is behavior that people so label.' This shifts analytical attention from why some individuals commit deviant acts (the question that strain theory and other 'cause of crime' frameworks address) to how acts and actors come to be labeled deviant in particular times and places. Lemert's distinction between primary deviance (initial rule-breaking, often experimental and not identity-defining) and secondary deviance (deviant behavior that follows from being publicly labeled and treated as deviant — what we might call 'becoming a criminal') was particularly influential. The framework emphasizes the role of moral entrepreneurs in creating and enforcing deviance categories, the differential distribution of labeling power (who gets labeled depends substantially on race, class, and other social factors), and the self-fulfilling-prophecy effects of labeling. Labeling theory had substantial influence on the deinstitutionalization movement and on policy reforms aimed at reducing labeling effects (juvenile-justice diversion, mental-health treatment alternatives), though empirical evidence on labeling effects is mixed.
originators: Howard S. Becker (foundational); Edwin Lemert (primary vs secondary deviance); Frank Tannenbaum (precursor 1938 'dramatization of evil'); Erving Goffman (Stigma 1963)
year_or_decade: 1938 (Tannenbaum precursor); 1951 (Lemert); 1963 (Becker Outsiders); 1960s flourishing
core_components: Deviance as social label rather than inherent property; Primary deviance (initial rule-breaking) vs secondary deviance (deviant identity post-labeling); Moral entrepreneurs; Differential distribution of labeling power; Self-fulfilling prophecy of labeling; Connection to symbolic interactionism; Influence on deinstitutionalization and diversion policies; Distinction from cause-of-crime theories (asks different question); Goffman's complementary work on stigma
primary_use_case: Sociology of deviance and criminology; foundation for substantial work on the criminal justice system, juvenile justice, and deinstitutionalization; reference framework in critical criminology; basis for policy advocacy around diversion and reduced labeling; influence on mental-health treatment philosophy; foundation for some social-movement analyses of stigmatized identities.
common_criticisms: Original framework was argued to underweight primary deviance (the initial rule-breaking) by focusing on labeling effects on subsequent behavior — strain, control, and learning theories better address why some commit primary deviance; empirical evidence on labeling effects is mixed — some studies show substantial effects of formal labeling on subsequent behavior, others show smaller effects than the framework predicts; risk of relativizing genuine harm by framing deviance as label rather than fact (strong-form readings have problematic implications for serious harm); differential labeling has substantial empirical support but the mechanisms are contested; commercial popularization has sometimes flattened the framework into 'don't label people'; tension between labeling theory's microsociological focus and the structural conditions producing differential labeling; integration with other criminological frameworks remains incomplete.
primary_sources: Lemert, E.M. (1951). Social Pathology; Becker, H.S. (1963). Outsiders: Studies in the Sociology of Deviance; Goffman, E. (1963). Stigma: Notes on the Management of Spoiled Identity
siblings: Strain Theory; Symbolic Interactionism; Goffman's Dramaturgy

name: Risk Society
one_line_summary: Beck's account of late modernity as organized around manufactured risks rather than scarcity.
extended_summary: Risk Society was articulated by Ulrich Beck in his 1986 Risikogesellschaft (English translation 1992 as Risk Society: Towards a New Modernity) and elaborated in subsequent works including World Risk Society (1999). Beck's central argument is that the dominant logic of modernity has shifted from the distribution of goods (the 'scarcity society' organizing around production and class conflict over material resources) to the distribution of bads — particularly manufactured risks produced as side effects of industrial modernity itself: nuclear-energy risks, environmental contamination, climate change, GMO risks, novel epidemics. These risks are characterized by being: invisible to direct sense; transboundary (don't respect national or class boundaries); produced by the success of industrial modernity rather than its failures; subject to social-scientific knowledge claims that are themselves contested; and creating new political dynamics that don't reduce to class. Beck distinguished 'first modernity' (industrial society, organized around classes) from 'second modernity' or 'reflexive modernization' (risk society, organized around manufactured risks and individualization). Beck's framework has been substantially influential in environmental sociology, science and technology studies, and discussions of late-modern political dynamics, with the COVID-19 pandemic offering substantial real-world illustration of risk-society dynamics. Critics have argued the framework is more programmatic than empirical, and that classical class and inequality concerns have not been displaced by risk in the way Beck claimed.
originators: Ulrich Beck
year_or_decade: 1986 (Risikogesellschaft, German); 1992 (English translation); 1999 (World Risk Society)
core_components: Shift from scarcity society (distribution of goods) to risk society (distribution of bads); Manufactured risks as side effects of industrial modernity; Risk characteristics: invisibility, transboundary nature, scientific contestability; Reflexive modernization; First vs second modernity; Individualization thesis; Connection to environmental sociology; Critique of classical class-conflict framings as adequate to contemporary social structure; Cosmopolitan implications of transboundary risks
primary_use_case: Environmental sociology and analysis of climate change, technological risk, nuclear policy, GMO controversy; foundation for substantial work on reflexive modernization; reference framework in late-modernity sociology; analysis of pandemics, financial crises, and other systemic risks; basis for arguments about cosmopolitan governance of transboundary risks; influence on STS and risk-perception research.
common_criticisms: More programmatic than empirically operationalized — Beck's grand thesis about modernity-shift is hard to test rigorously; classical class and inequality concerns have not been displaced by risk in the way Beck claimed (classical inequality continues to drive much social conflict, and risks are themselves unequally distributed); individualization thesis has been challenged as overstating the dissolution of class structures; reflexive-modernization claim that society has become reflexively aware of its own risks has been argued to be optimistic about deliberative capacity; the framework's European context shaped specific framings that don't always travel; tension between Beck's later cosmopolitan turn and the framework's original European focus; commercial and academic popularization has produced 'risk society' as label without engaging the systematic theoretical commitments; competition with other late-modernity framings (Bauman's liquid modernity, Giddens's reflexive modernization) creates which-when ambiguity.
primary_sources: Beck, U. (1986). Risikogesellschaft (English: 1992, Risk Society: Towards a New Modernity); Beck, U. (1999). World Risk Society; Beck, U., Giddens, A. & Lash, S. (1994). Reflexive Modernization

name: Liquid Modernity
one_line_summary: Bauman's framework characterizing the present as fluid, individualized, and unsettled.
extended_summary: Liquid Modernity was articulated by Polish-British sociologist Zygmunt Bauman in his 2000 book of that name, with subsequent elaborations in Liquid Love (2003), Liquid Life (2005), Liquid Times (2007), Consuming Life (2007), and Liquid Fear (2006). Bauman characterizes the contemporary phase of modernity as 'liquid' in contrast to earlier 'solid' modernity — solid modernity (roughly the 19th and 20th centuries through approximately 1970) was structured by relatively stable institutions, predictable life trajectories, lifelong jobs, durable commitments, and collective identities; liquid modernity is characterized by fluidity, fragmentation, individualization, perpetual transformation, deinstitutionalization, mobility, and the inability of any particular form to hold its shape over time. Key features include: the privatization of risk (individual responsibility for managing risks that were previously social); consumerism as identity (we are what we consume, and consumption is restless); the disposability of relationships, jobs, and identities; the difficulty of long-term commitments; and the disorienting acceleration of social change. Bauman's framework has substantial overlap with Beck's risk society and Giddens's late modernity but with a distinctively bleaker tone — Bauman is principally a critic rather than analyst of liquid modernity. The framework has influenced cultural criticism, sociology of consumption, and contemporary discussions of digital and social-media-mediated life, though it has drawn critique for being more aphoristic than rigorously argued and for romanticizing the more-stable solid modernity it contrasts with.
originators: Zygmunt Bauman
year_or_decade: 2000 (Liquid Modernity); subsequent 'Liquid' series 2003-2007
core_components: Liquid vs solid modernity distinction; Fluidity, fragmentation, individualization as defining features; Privatization of risk; Consumerism as identity; Disposability of relationships, jobs, identities; Difficulty of long-term commitment; Acceleration of social change; Distinction from but overlap with Beck's risk society and Giddens's late modernity; Critical rather than analytic stance; Application to consumer culture, digital life, contemporary intimacy
primary_use_case: Cultural criticism and sociology of contemporary life; analysis of consumer culture, digital and social-media life, and contemporary intimacy; reference framework in late-modernity sociology; basis for substantial commentary on contemporary cultural moods; influence on critical theory and political theology discussions of the present; foundation for some pastoral and therapeutic engagement with contemporary disorientation.
common_criticisms: More aphoristic than rigorously argued — Bauman's prolific late output produced striking metaphors and characterizations but limited systematic theoretical development; romanticizes solid modernity as more stable and unified than it actually was — the 'solid' period also had substantial mobility, instability, and individualization that the contrast obscures; cross-cultural application is limited — the European-Western framing shapes specific characterizations; tension between descriptive and critical aspects of Bauman's project (is liquidity bad in itself or only in some forms?); difficult to operationalize empirically — what would count as evidence for or against the framework?; competition with other late-modernity framings creates terminological proliferation without clear analytical advantage; popular adoption sometimes uses 'liquid' as buzzword for any contemporary instability without engaging Bauman's specific framework.
primary_sources: Bauman, Z. (2000). Liquid Modernity; Bauman, Z. (2003). Liquid Love; Bauman, Z. (2007). Liquid Times: Living in an Age of Uncertainty

name: World-Systems Theory
one_line_summary: Wallerstein's framework of core, periphery, and semi-periphery in the global capitalist system.
extended_summary: World-Systems Theory was developed by Immanuel Wallerstein and presented in The Modern World-System Volume I: Capitalist Agriculture and the Origins of the European World-Economy in the Sixteenth Century (1974), with three subsequent volumes through 2011. Wallerstein argued that the proper unit of analysis for understanding the modern world is not the nation-state or society but the world-system — a single capitalist world-economy that emerged in 16th-century Europe and progressively incorporated the rest of the globe. The world-system is structured by an international division of labor producing three structural positions: core (high-wage, high-technology, capital-intensive production; powerful states; Western Europe, North America, Japan); periphery (low-wage, low-technology, raw-material extraction; weak states; much of Africa, Latin America, Southeast Asia historically); and semi-periphery (intermediate position, often serving as buffer; some Latin American and East Asian economies). Wallerstein drew on Marx, Fernand Braudel's longue durée historiography, and Andre Gunder Frank's dependency theory. The framework has had substantial influence on global sociology, international political economy, and historical sociology, providing a structural alternative to modernization theory's account of development as nation-state-bounded process. Critics have argued that World-Systems Theory underweights internal sources of social change, treats the world-economy too monolithically, and is more descriptive than predictive about specific national trajectories.
originators: Immanuel Wallerstein; intellectual antecedents in Karl Marx, Fernand Braudel, Andre Gunder Frank (dependency theory)
year_or_decade: 1974 (Volume I); ongoing development through 2011 (Volume IV)
core_components: World-system as unit of analysis (not nation-state or society); Capitalist world-economy emerging in 16th-century Europe; Three structural positions: core, periphery, semi-periphery; International division of labor; Unequal exchange and value transfer from periphery to core; Hegemonic cycles (Dutch, British, American); Antisystemic movements; Connection to dependency theory; Distinction from modernization theory's nation-state-bounded development account
primary_use_case: Global and historical sociology; international political economy; analysis of development and underdevelopment; reference framework in critical international relations; basis for substantial work on globalization, hegemonic cycles, and inequality between nations; foundation for some neo-Marxist analyses of contemporary capitalism; influence on world-historical scholarship.
common_criticisms: Treats world-economy too monolithically — internal national and regional variation in development trajectories don't always fit neatly into core-periphery framework; East Asian developmental states (Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, China) substantially complicated the framework's predictions about peripheral development; underweights internal sources of social change in particular societies; descriptively powerful but less predictive about specific national trajectories; overlap with and competing claims against dependency theory and Marxist political economy; methodological challenges in operationalizing core-periphery measures; cross-disciplinary tension between sociologists and economists about the framework's empirical adequacy; semi-periphery category sometimes seems to be defined residually; commercial popularization has produced 'world systems' as buzzword without engaging Wallerstein's specific theoretical commitments.
primary_sources: Wallerstein, I. (1974). The Modern World-System Vol I; Wallerstein, I. (2004). World-Systems Analysis: An Introduction; Frank, A.G. (1966). 'The Development of Underdevelopment' (dependency-theory precursor)

name: Theory of Communicative Action
one_line_summary: Habermas' framework distinguishing instrumental from communicative rationality.
extended_summary: Jürgen Habermas's Theory of Communicative Action was articulated in his two-volume Theorie des kommunikativen Handelns (1981, English translation 1984-1987) and is the principal second-generation Frankfurt-School reformulation of Critical Theory. Habermas distinguished four types of action: teleological/instrumental (oriented to success in achieving goals through control of objects); strategic (instrumental action oriented to success in influencing other actors as objects); norm-regulative (oriented to compliance with shared norms); and communicative (oriented to mutual understanding through unconstrained reasoned argumentation). Communicative rationality — embedded in the implicit validity claims of speech acts (truth, normative rightness, sincerity, comprehensibility) — provides the foundation for democratic legitimacy and rational social order, and is normatively prior to instrumental rationality. The 'system' (economy and state, organized by money and power) and the 'lifeworld' (the everyday domain of communicative action and shared meaning) coexist in modern societies, but the 'colonization of the lifeworld' by system-imperatives represents pathologies of modernity. Habermas's framework substantially repositioned Critical Theory away from the first generation's pessimism (Dialectic of Enlightenment) and toward a normative grounding in the implicit rationality of communication. The framework has had enormous influence in social theory, political theory (deliberative democracy), legal theory (procedural justification), and ethics (discourse ethics). Critics including Foucault, Lyotard, and feminists have argued that the appeal to ideal communication abstracts from power and difference in problematic ways.
originators: Jürgen Habermas
year_or_decade: 1981 (Theorie des kommunikativen Handelns, German); 1984-1987 (English translation)
core_components: Four action types: teleological/instrumental, strategic, norm-regulative, communicative; Communicative rationality grounded in validity claims (truth, rightness, sincerity, comprehensibility); System (money and power) vs lifeworld (communicative action); Colonization of the lifeworld; Discourse ethics (Diskursethik); Ideal speech situation; Foundation for deliberative democracy; Distinction from first-generation Frankfurt School pessimism; Connection to broader project of grounding critical theory in rational communication
primary_use_case: Social and political theory; foundation for deliberative-democracy theory and practice; basis for substantial work in democratic theory, public-sphere analysis, and political legitimacy; influence on legal theory (procedural justification of democratic legitimacy); foundation for discourse ethics; reference framework in critical theory's second generation; influence on practical applications including stakeholder dialogue, deliberative polling, and public engagement design.
common_criticisms: Ideal speech situation and unconstrained communication abstractions have been argued to abstract from real power asymmetries that make ideal conditions unattainable; Foucault's critique that the appeal to communication-as-foundation underweights how power-knowledge produces what counts as rational; feminist critiques (Iris Marion Young, Seyla Benhabib) that the rationality criteria embed culturally specific norms about argument that exclude other communicative modes (story, testimony, rhetoric); postmodern critiques (Lyotard) of grand-narrative grounding in rationality; substantial complexity of the framework limits accessibility; tension between Habermas's substantive engagement with empirical social science and his normative-philosophical grounding; the practical operationalization of deliberative democracy in actual political institutions has been mixed; cross-cultural application of European-grounded framing.
primary_sources: Habermas, J. (1981). Theorie des kommunikativen Handelns; Habermas, J. (1984-1987). The Theory of Communicative Action (English translation, 2 vols); Habermas, J. (1990). Moral Consciousness and Communicative Action
